en: Treatise on the True Reality of the Benevolent Kings’ Prajñāpāramitā, Scroll 20.3. [Fragmentary Text]. ...
Various Clarities... Eightfold Cultivation of Ritual Offerings.

□□□□□□□□□□□□□□□□ Prajñāpāramitā, [the *Buddhāvataṃsaka*,] the *Ratnaketuparipṛcchā*, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, and others; the practice of making offerings to the *vipāka-buddhas* (buddhas of retribution) through contemplation. □□□□□□□□□ Reaching the completion of the single flower pedestal (*ekapuṣpa-vitāna*), the practice of cultivating the Dharma and making offerings to the Three Jewels through the contemplation of the various kings and others upon the *dharmatā-buddhas*. □□□□□□□□□ The Buddhas of the ten directions and the devas scatter flowers.
Regarding the reason why this scriptural passage has come forth:
the answer is that it clarifies that after the various kings and others have completed their cultivation of meritorious practices,
they further wish to give rise to vows.
Therefore, the meditative practice is summarized as being unobstructed and unhindered,
pervading the great earth.
The essence is true, [and so on], descending like clouds;
for this reason, there is this scriptural passage. Furthermore, another interpretation is as follows:
"Immeasurable joy" clarifies the offering of mental action; that is,
scattering hundreds of billions of flowers which descend like clouds.
This clarifies the offering of physical action.
The three [sections] range from the past Buddhas according to their vows up to the *prajñāpāramitā*.
This clarifies the offering of verbal karma.
Following the section on supernatural transformations, it describes the three types of worlds below;
from a single flower, one enters into immeasurable flowers.
"Even entering into a mustard seed" clarifies that the Pure Land is of one essence with the world;
it is the world of Perfect Enlightenment.
Second, as for "entering from the body of one Buddha into the bodies of immeasurable sentient beings, even unto the bodies of the six destinies":
this refers to the world of sentient beings within the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*).
As for "entering earth, water, fire, and wind": [this refers to the world of the vessel].
The phrase "the Buddha-body is inconceivable" clarifies the world of the land;
it concludes the preceding section on the world of perfect enlightenment.
"Sentient beings are inconceivable" refers to the aforementioned twenty-five realms of existence within the world of sentient beings.
"The world is inconceivable" refers to... [the realm of the vessel-world].
This concludes the section on the World of Sentient Beings and the World of the Environment.
At that time, the sixteen great kings who heard the Buddha preach the *Prajñāpāramitā* in one hundred trillion verses were filled with joy.
Because the essence is in accord with joy, it is called "rejoicing.
As for the scattering of hundreds of thousands of billions of flower stalks, this refers to the Dharma.
The present mind constitutes the practice.
The meaning of "practice" having a cause is called "flower.
The application of practice is not singular; it is termed "scattering."
Thus it is said that "one million billion flowers were scattered,
which transformed into a single seat in mid-air.
This reveals that unobstructed practice is in perfect accord with the equality of space.
The statement that "the Buddhas of the ten directions sit together to expound the Prajñā" clarifies the two paths of realization and teaching;
they are "together" in their non-duality.
Sitting is the Way of Realization (sākṣātkriyāmārga),
while speaking is the Way of Teaching (deśanāmārga).
Therefore, it is said that they sit together in the Prajñāpāramitā.
As for the immeasurable multitude sitting together on one seat:
although they dwell at the stage of training,
their essence is non-dual.
"Golden *kora* flowers scattered upon Śākyamuni" manifests the shared causal practice:
although its essential nature is pliant and functions in accordance with conditions, its fundamental character remains unaltered.
Therefore, it is said that he took *jinaruha* flowers and scattered them over Śākyamuni Buddha,
and further scattered eighty-four thousand *prajñāpāramitā* flowers into the midst of space.
That it transforms into a White Cloud Terrace illustrates the causal practice of the purity of nature.
The thundering roar and the flowers [symbolize]...
The "Flower of Prior Limits" refers to the practice of teaching and conduct in the past.
The "Flower of Sublime Enlightenment" refers to the practice of the fruit in the future.
The "Flower of Gods and Humans" refers to the practice of worldly retribution and the practice of skillful means.

Indeed, although the preliminary expedients (*pūrvayoga*) of scattering sand from the Ganges River [before the Buddha] were the same for both gods and humans, because all worldly phenomena are the true *prajñā*, it is said that the *prajñā* explained below... (the word "etc. [or "and so forth"] is used).
Because it is the fruit of one's own essential nature, it is called the "mother.
Regarding the place of birth through supernormal powers (*abhijñā*):
although it is real, it is characterized by neither signs nor signlessness.
Being sovereign and unimpeded,
it is called the "place where supernatural powers arise.
At that time, the Buddha manifested five inconceivable things for the king.
This manifests the Tathāgata’s fulfillment of the practice of the five patiences (*kṣānti*).
As for the three kinds of *dharmakāya*,
they are manifested to reveal that the path cultivated removes the three obstructions.
The five kinds of inconceivability clarify the unimpeded nature of the causal path;
the three bodies clarify the resultant path.
That a single flower enters into immeasurable flowers and immeasurable flowers enter into a single flower is the unimpeded practice of self-benefit.
That a single buddha-field enters into immeasurable buddha-fields [is likewise].
As for "immeasurable buddha-fields entering a single buddha-field," this directly clarifies that the substance of the fields is without obstruction.
It further describes immeasurable buddha-fields entering a single pore of the skin.
The entry of the earth within a single pore into the earth of immeasurable pores clarifies that which is vast and unobstructed.
That immeasurable Mount Sumerus and immeasurable great oceans enter into a single mustard seed— [clarifies the same].
This clarifies that there is no obstruction between the large and the small.
Thus it is said: "Immeasurable Mount Sumerus and immeasurable great oceans enter into a single mustard seed;
even the body of a single Buddha, and indeed bodies of earth, water, fire, and wind, likewise enter [into one another]."
This clarifies the primary retribution.
That the Buddha-body is inconceivable refers to the practice of not abandoning birth and death.
That the bodies of sentient beings are inconceivable means they do not abandon the practice of *nirvāṇa*.
That worlds are inconceivable—
The Dharma-realm is the practice of non-obstruction.
Regarding the "Chapter on Receiving and Upholding," the question is asked:
"In making offerings by scattering flowers, the fused characteristics are equal."
How does the arising of practice enable its circulation?
The answer is:
the thirteen great beings cultivate contemplation and give rise to understanding.
One who has accomplished the virtues of practice is then able to disseminate [the teaching].
Within this chapter, there are three sections.
The scriptural text begins from the opening until the section on the Path of the Dharma of Emptiness,
wherein King Candraprabha poses his questions.
Second, it extends from the words of the Great Muni until the passage on upholding the Prajñāpāramitā-mantra.
Answering their questions,
from the third section on "The Time" through the end of the chapter,
it elucidates the path for those who have attained awakening.
Within the section on the posing of questions,
there are two lines of scripture beginning from "At that time, King Candraprabha..."
Each then spoke of the Prajñāpāramitā,
clarifying the profound and wondrous deeds practiced by the Buddhas within the minds of the Vidyārājas.
The two then addressed the Buddha, saying:
When the path of the Dharma of emptiness was opened and he was about to formally pose his question with his own mouth,
at that time King Candraprabha had this thought in his mind:
This refers back to the three kinds of dharmakāya mentioned in the preceding chapter.
As for "speaking with the mouth," this precisely reveals the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa).
First, to clarify what is being contemplated,
it says: "one speaks with the mouth" when seeing Śākyamuni.
This reveals the skillful means:
the Dharma-body does not abandon the world while realizing nirvana;
therefore, it is said that one "sees Śākyamuni."
As for the manifestation of immeasurable spiritual powers:
one also sees the Buddha Ratnapūrṇa upon the thousand-petaled lotus pedestal;
he is the master of the transformation bodies of all Buddhas.
Without abandoning nirvana, one gathers profound functions.
Those who see the Buddha in the world are beholding the Dharma-realm body (dharmadhātu-kāya).
He addressed the Buddha, which refers to his verbal explanation.
That such Prajñāpāramitā is ineffable is because the path of language has been severed.
That which is called "ineffable" and "incomprehensible" cannot be fathomed by those of the Two Vehicles.
Therefore, it is said that it cannot be understood;
that which cannot be discussed through discussion is beyond the reach of ordinary beings.
Therefore it is said that it is not cognized by consciousness.
A question is asked: "The true nature of Prajñā transcends the path of language."
The sphere of mental activity ceases.
How can one be said to possess virtuous conduct?
Sons of good family who deeply understand this according to the Dharma [are so].
It is for the sake of all sentient beings to reveal and develop the wondrous path of signless quiescence.
He replied:
There are thirteen great beings who possess the dharma-gate of true contemplation and are able to propagate it.
Within the response, there are two phrases of scripture.
The first briefly and generally mentions the Dharma-preacher’s practice of tranquility and exhorts one to offer worship.
Second, from "Good son" up to "prajñāpāramitā," it extensively distinguishes the two types of practice and intention: internal protection and external protection.
The statement that there are "only thirteen" refers specifically to the Tathāgata;
this is according to the second division [of the text].
There are two phrases in the sūtra text:
"As for that Dharma master,
he is as unshakable as a whetted blade."
This clarifies the virtue of practicing internal protection.
Second, from the Buddha’s address to King Prasenajit until the point of upholding the *prajñāpāramitā*.
This clarifies the virtue of external protection.

Within the practice of internal protection, there are two phrases of the sūtra: first, it clarifies that the thirteen practices of the Dharma masters are accomplished through the power of intention, such that they are capable of understanding and capable of expounding [the teachings].

Second, from "O son of good family, such bodhisattvas" up to "are equal and without distinction," this section collectively enumerates the thirteen Dharma masters who are endowed with superior conduct and virtue.
This can be well understood through examination.
Within each section, there are two phrases.
From the beginning up to this point, these refer to those of indeterminate status.
This clarifies the practice of entering through the cultivation of skillful means as an antidote.
Second, regarding those who enter from this meditative concentration:
they reach the stage of *saṃghāta*.
This clarifies the virtues of accomplishing practice.
When the Dharma Master of the Stage of Cultivating the Seeds first contemplates earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness,
he is contemplating the impurity of the six great elements.
Next, regarding the contemplation of the fourteen faculties:
one contemplates that these fourteen faculties are impure;
they possess only conditioned marks.
Without manifesting the eight untainted [attainments],
they constantly cultivate the three realms up to the gate of the contemplation of impurity,
observing the three realms.
Because conditioned things are defiled and turbid, they are collectively termed "impure";
hence it is called the "Gate of the Contemplation of Impurity.
Those who abide in the Buddha's household [should practice this].
Believing that one's mind takes True Suchness (tathatā) as its home,
it is said that one "dwells in the Buddha’s family.
To practice the six points of harmonious respect (ṣaḍ-vidha-sāmīcī):
Practicing loving-kindness through the three karmas, sharing the same precepts and the same views,
and studying the eighty-four thousand *prajñāpāramitās*—
these constitute the joint cultivation of the eighty-four thousand practices.

Regarding the nature of the stage of cultivation (*śikṣā-bīja-gotra*): it refers to those persons who have newly begun to cultivate and enter into the principle and wisdom (*li-ji*), and who have a slight understanding that their own bodies possess this nature;
therefore, it is called the nature of the stage of cultivation.
Those who have entered the stage of the emptiness of persons practice the contemplation of the non-self of the person and do not commit the five heinous crimes.
The Sūtra states: "Parents are the field of gratitude;
Arhats, the Saṃgha, and the Buddha are the field of merit.
One should not give rise to hostility or inflict harm upon these two fields."
Therefore, it is said that one does not rise to greet or oppose.
Regarding "not giving rise to the six grave offenses," this means not violating the four prohibitions.
One does not sell alcohol,
nor does one speak of the faults or transgressions of the fourfold assembly;
therefore, it is said that one does not give rise to the six grave offenses.
Regarding the twenty-eight minor precepts:
according to the Brahmajāla Sūtra, there are forty-eight minor precepts,
beginning from the time one first intends to accept the position of a king.
The position of a Wheel-Turning King;
the positions of the hundred officials;
at that time.
One should receive the Bodhisattva precepts.
All ghosts and spirits will protect the king’s person and protect the persons of the hundred officials;
all Buddhas will rejoice.
They do not rise to greet or prostrate before their preceptors (upādhyāya), ācāryas, or great fellow-students;
nor do they provide them with offerings of the seven precious gems and foods of a hundred flavors in accordance with the Dharma.
If one does not do so, one commits a minor offense (light impurity).
This applies even to those who have received the precepts with a sincere heart.
If kings, crown princes, officials, or disciples of the fourfold assembly,
relying on their own high status and nobility,
seek to destroy and break the Buddha-dharma;
I shall restrain my disciples,
not permitting them to leave the household life to practice the Way,
nor allowing them to fashion images, construct stūpas, or produce the sūtras and vinaya.
One who acts in this way commits a minor offense.
To claim that the Buddhist scriptures constitute an act of rebellion by asserting they were not spoken by the Buddha—
there is no such possibility.
Birth is not incidental.
One who is able to cultivate and subdue patience throughout one asaṃkhyeya kalpa clarifies the stages of practice through the kalpas.
Those who first enter the stage of *saṃghāṭa* are here called those of the "nature of cultivated seeds" (*xi zhongxing*).
Within this category of the nature of seeds, there are two phrases of sutra text.
From the beginning until every thought-moment, it does not depart from the mind;
this clarifies the practice of remedial skillful means.
Second, from the two *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
Upon reaching the stage of *pāramitā-vihāra*,
one clearly accomplishes the qualities of practice.
As for the "nature-lineage" (*gotra*):
The essence of the white [nature] can manifest its own inherent nature;
therefore, it is called "lineage" (*gotra*).
As for "nature," it refers to the principle of the direct cause, which serves as the seed for the fruit of Buddhahood.
It is not produced from causes,
nor is it destroyed by things; therefore,
it is called the "nature-lineage" (*prakṛtisthagotra*).
The contemplation of the ten unwholesome actions that extinguishes the ten inversions is the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness.
Eliminating the inversions of permanence, bliss, self, and purity;
through the contemplation of compassion and benevolence,
one eliminates greed, hatred, and delusion.
One performs the contemplation of causes and conditions to eliminate the afflictions of annihilationism, eternalism, pleasure, and self; therefore,

it is said that by practicing the ten kinds of wisdom-contemplations, one extinguishes the ten inversions as well as [the notions of] self and person, up to the cultivation and protection of the contemplation of emptiness.
Once contemplation is perfected,
provisional marks do not arise; therefore,
it is said that they are "non-existent."
Furthermore, those who constantly practice the hundred thousand pāramitās, never departing from them in thought after thought,
resolve their minds on practice that penetrates to the very end of time;
having practiced the Dharma of the right path for two asaṃkhyeya kalpas of the world, they proceed to the stage of the pāramitās.
The Wei [dynasty] translation calls it the "nature-seed" (*gotra*). Hence it is said to be the stage of *pāramitā*.
As for the "path-seed nature," it can serve as the path for the first [stage].
Therefore, it is called the "nature of the lineage of the path.
To observe that all phenomena are without arising, abiding,
or ceasing clarifies the emptiness of the three marks.
This refers to the five types of feeling;
it means contemplating the emptiness of the five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādāna-skandha).
This is because [these aggregates] cannot be apprehended, from the three realms up to the ultimate limit.
This clarifies that both the two emperors of the triple world are suchness.
Regarding the "Eighth Constant," the First Noble Truth,
it is the object of contemplation within the phrase.
The foremost is the Sovereign of Ultimate Meaning (Paramārtharāja).
His mind is tranquil and extinguished in every thought-moment;
yet those born within the three realms have not yet ceased their bondage to karma.
Therefore, it is said that one undergoes birth within the three realms.
As for "the karmic habituation and its retribution," this refers to the residual traces of bound karma.
Regarding "born in accordance with the Way":
they are born truly by virtue of the power of their vows;
therefore, it is said they are "born in accordance with the Way."
Having practiced the eighty thousand koṭis of prajñāpāramitās for three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, one who dwells in the stage of avaivartika realizes the state of non-retrogression.
Within the stage of the Joyful Ground (*pramuditā-bhūmi*),
there are two scriptural passages.
From the beginning up to "all pure lands," these clarify the practice of remedial skillful means (*pratipakṣa-upāya-caryā*).
Second, because of constantly cultivating the contemplation of equanimity,
one reaches the stage of constant bestowal.
Seventh, this clarifies the virtue of accomplishing matured conduct.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, who dwells in the patience of equanimity (samatā-kṣānti),
clarifies that the Great Being of the first stage, the Joyful (pramuditā-bhūmi), possesses the lower grade of the patience of faith (śraddhā-kṣānti);
therefore, it is said that he dwells in the patience of equanimity.
"Practicing the four means of integration,
with every thought-moment never departing from the mind" clarifies that this Bodhisattva has newly ascended into the stage of true realization of the mark of non-arising.
One practices the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*).
Because one is fully endowed with all virtuous qualities internally and externally, both for oneself and others,
it is said that one practices the four means of integration, never allowing them to depart from the mind even for a single thought-moment.
Entering the signless and abandoning the afflictions of greed within the three realms clarifies the practice of relinquishing and embracing the truth.
Because the signs of conditions do not defile him,
it is said that he enters the signless (animitta).
He abandons and extinguishes the afflictions such as craving within the three realms.
"Non-dual with respect to the ultimate truth" clarifies the realization of the equality of true emptiness.
"Encompassing the unconditioned dharma-nature of sentient beings" refers to...
Excluding the obstruction of its own nature reveals true reality.
To extinguish [the afflictions] by taking principle as the object, up to the signless and the unconditioned, is [the meaning].
It eliminates the cognitive hindrances.
When abiding in the first stage of patience (*kṣānti*),
up until the unconditioned state of signlessness (*animitta*) which is non-intellectually-dependent cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
This eliminates the hindrance of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "because there is neither the mark of self and other nor the absence of marks," this is intended to clarify the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*).
"Beyond these three obstructions, one possesses the three unconditioned states.
"Immeasurable skillful means all manifest before one's observation" refers to the arising of the six kinds of skillful means practices of the lower stage.
The skillful means of the true mark is real wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).
From "in the ultimate sense" up to "not inverted," this clarifies the functioning of real wisdom.
Second, from the training in all things (*sarvaśikṣā*) to the training in everything (*sarvaśikṣā*):
this clarifies that the skillful means of training in all things is precisely the path of non-going (*agati*).
Third, the skillful means of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-upāya*).
Because it is dedicated toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), it is called the "expedient means of dedication.
Regarding the "expedient means of mastery over the four māras":
it is to practice the Buddha-way within what is not the way.
Yet they are not moved by the four māras.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "To practice on what is not the Path and yet penetrate the Buddha-path" is precisely the realization.
Regarding the fifth, the skillful means of the One Vehicle:
it is the thorough penetration of the dharma-realm and of sentient beings within the state of non-duality.
Being free from all hindrances,
it is therefore called the "expedient means of the One Vehicle.
Sixth, the expedient means of transformation:
By the power of their vows,
they manifest births at will in various places; therefore,
it is called the "expedient means of transformation."
Good son, this forms six kinds of skillful means.

From the initial wisdom of investigation and analysis up to the illumination of true wisdom, the first phrase above is concluded: the skillful application of the means of true wisdom that does not realize [nirvana].
"Summarizing the preceding skillful means of universal study;
'not out of sequence' summarizes the preceding skillful means of dedication;
'not emerging' summarizes the preceding skillful means of the mastery of Māra."
Regarding the "Non-erroneous," this concludes the sixth section on the skillful means of transformation;
it is not separately concluded because the fifth section on the skillful means of the One Vehicle shares the same characteristics.
This is like the analogy that water and its waves are neither identical nor different.
This provides an analogy for the skillful means of ultimate wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).
"Entering this gateway of the treasury of merit" concludes the six kinds of practices regarding the quiescent and active functions of skillful means.
Those who have no further arising from the karmic habit-energies of the three realms, and who constantly cultivate the contemplation of equanimity,
thereby severing their bonds and entering the signless state;
those who abandon and extinguish the afflictions of greed within the three realms and ascend to the stage of Kumārabhūta.
The preceding section on the Bodhisattva Suprabuddha,
who constantly bestows the four great treasures upon others,
clarifies that the bodhisattva always employs the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) to transform sentient beings.
Because there is no seeking,
it is said that the four great treasuries are constantly bestowed upon people.
This summarizes the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), which are never absent from the mind at any moment.
Within the Vimalā-bhūmi (The Stainless Ground), there are two scriptural passages.
From the beginning up to the section on "dwelling in contemplation," these clarify the practice of skillful means as an antidote.
Second, from the five *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas until the transformation of all sentient beings,
this clarifies the intention for accomplishing matured practice.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Virtuous Beneficence (Guṇamati) is the Bodhisattva Free from Defilement (Vimala).
He resembles the four immeasurable minds (apramāṇacitta).
One cultivates the ten wholesome deeds oneself and teaches others to practice the ten wholesome deeds.
Since the four immeasurables are the root of all these virtues,
it is said that one employs the four immeasurable minds.
Regarding those who extinguish the afflictions such as hatred within the three realms:
among the ten non-virtuous actions, the ripening karma of the first action may arise from certain causes.
Now, it is intended to demonstrate that the karma of non-killing serves as the antidote to the karma of killing.
Therefore, it is said that "hatred and other afflictions are extinguished.
As for "the afflictions abiding within medium patience," this refers to the medium grade of the stage of patient acceptance (*kṣānti*).
Regarding "practicing all meritorious virtues":
by cultivating the purity of the three karmas, there is no virtue that is not perfected;
therefore, one practices all meritorious virtues.
"Contemplating the mind with great compassion;
the mind is always present before one" summarizes the aforementioned four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*).
One who enters the *śatadharā* of signlessness practices the penetrating contemplation of signlessness and realizes the Stainless Stage (*vimalā-bhūmi*).
Therefore, it is said that one enters the *niḥsābha-jñāta-pāramitā*.
Within the third stage, the Illuminating Ground (*prabhākari-bhūmi*),
this refers to the period from the beginning until the attainment of all meritorious qualities through the contemplation of the three types of higher knowledge (*trividyā*).
This clarifies the practice of the skillful means of the antidote.
Second, one constantly employs the six *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas until the upholding of all dharmas is attained.
This clarifies the virtue of maturing conduct.
Furthermore, regarding the entry into the path of wisdom,
this clarifies that the Bodhisattva of the third stage is vast and extensively learned.
Because one preaches the Dharma for sentient beings and is able to provide illumination,
it is called the entry into the path of clear wisdom.
Those who constantly practice the contemplation of the three insights within the patience of signlessness possess the supreme wisdom of faithful patience,
for they give rise to their practice therein without conceptual discrimination.
This refers to the patience of signlessness (*animitta-kṣānti*).
He skillfully enters the eight dhyānas and roams his spirit within the four immeasurables;
his five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) are unimpeded.
Because he clearly illuminates the three periods of time, his speech and practice constitute the observation of the three types of higher knowledge (*traividya*);
he knows that the phenomena of the three periods have no coming, no going, and no place of abiding in the present.
Regarding "the mind and mind are stilled":
as the spirit becomes increasingly tranquil, its illumination becomes ever more brilliant;
hence it is said that "the mind and mind are stilled."
Regarding "exhausting the delusive afflictions of the three realms":
because the darkness of ignorance obscures the mind and blocks the eye of wisdom, one exhausts them.

Regarding "attaining the three types of supernormal knowledge (trividyā) and all meritorious qualities through the contemplation of the delusive afflictions of the three realms": [this refers to the attainment of these states].
Once the signs of darkness have ceased,
true illumination shines forth clearly,
and all virtues are cultivated purely.
Therefore, it is said that one attains the three insights (*tisro vidyāḥ*) by means of contemplating all meritorious qualities;
this immediately re-establishes the aforementioned contemplation of insight.
This is practiced constantly throughout six *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
The "Accumulation of the Perfection of Immeasurable Radiance" refers to the stages of virtuous conduct spanning kalpas;
it is also called the period of practice when one enters the stage of *kalāpa*.
Regarding those who uphold all dharmas through the practice of signlessness,
this again constitutes the aforementioned "constantly abiding in the patience of signlessness" within the context of the fourth stage (bhūmi).
This clarifies two phrases of the sūtra text.
From the beginning up to "extinguishing all views of the three realms," it clarifies the practice of remedial skillful means.
Second, from another seven *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas until reaching the stage of "never being separated from the mind," it clarifies the accomplishment of the virtues of practice.
Furthermore, as for the Bodhisattva Āryajñānaprabhākara,
this Mahāsattva of the fourth stage possesses the lower grade of *anulomikī-kṣānti*;
his practice of non-giving, upholding the precepts, and extensive learning increase further.
Its majestic power is blazing and intense;
it is named the "Blazing Ground" (Arciṣmatī).
It is for those who turn back the current of the five views.
The Great Being of the Fourth Ground contemplates the factors of the path and so forth,
yet does not maintain the notion of one who can understand or enter them.
Because no views arise,
it is said that one "flows against the current of the five views.
As for "accumulating immeasurable merit":
Because their path, conduct, virtue, precepts, concentration, and wisdom are fully perfected without deficiency,
they are said to possess immeasurable merit;
such are those who abide in the stage of *srotāpanna*.
The Sūtra states: "In the language of Qin, it is called 'Contemplating the Radiant Ground.

During the time when the Buddha was in the world, there were also military slaves who left the household life.
For what reason, in later generations, is the ordination of military slaves considered an evil practice?
